'''Bradley Efron''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɛ|f|r|ən}}; born May 24, 1938)<ref>[http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~ckirby/brad/EfronCV.pdf Bradley Efron Curriculum Vitae]  {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100818003431/http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~ckirby/brad/EfronCV.pdf}}</ref> is an American statistician. Efron has been president of the [[American Statistical Association]] (2004) and of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] (1987–1988).<ref name="AMSNews">Cochran, J. (1&nbsp;September 2015), "ASA Leaders Reminisce: Brad Efron", ''Amstat News''.</ref> He is a past editor (for theory and methods) of the ''[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]'', and he is the founding editor of the ''[[Annals of Applied Statistics]]''.<ref name="AMSNews" /> Efron is also the recipient of many awards (see below).

Efron is especially known for proposing the [[Bootstrapping (statistics)|bootstrap resampling technique]],<ref>{{cite journal |url = http://projecteuclid.org/DPubS?service=UI&version=1.0&verb=Display&handle=euclid.aos/1176344552 | title = Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife | journal = The Annals of Statistics | volume = 7 |issue=1 |pages = 1–26| doi = 10.1214/aos/1176344552|year = 1979|last1 = Efron|first1 = B.|doi-access = free}}</ref> which has had a major impact in the field of [[statistics]] and virtually every area of statistical application. The bootstrap was one of the first computer-intensive statistical techniques, replacing traditional [[algebra]]ic derivations with data-based computer simulations.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Efron, Bradley|title=A 250-year argument: Belief, behavior, and the bootstrap|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)|year=2013|volume=50|issue=1|pages=129–146|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-2012-01374-5|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Efron was born in [[St. Paul, Minnesota]] in May 1938, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants Esther and Miles Efron.<ref>{{cite web|title=Efron to Speak on Baseball, Shakespeare, and Modern Statistical Theory|year=2007|website=[[Joint Mathematics Meetings|Joint Mathematics Meetings 2007]]|publisher=American Mathematical Society|url=https://jointmathematicsmeetings.org/meetings/national/jmm/2098_intro.html}}</ref> He attended the [[California Institute of Technology]], graduating in mathematics in 1960. By his own admission he "had no talent for modern abstract math". His interest in statistics emerged after reading a [[Harald Cramér]] book cover to cover.<ref>McClave, James T., and Terry Sincich. "Statistics, 1 1t h Edition." (2009).</ref> Soon later, he arrived at [[Stanford]] in fall of 1960, earning his Ph.D., under the direction of Rupert Miller and [[Herbert Solomon]], in the Department of Statistics.  While at Stanford, he was suspended for six months for his involvement with the ''[[Stanford Chaparral]]'''s parody of ''[[Playboy]]'' magazine.<ref>{{cite web
|url = http://content.cdlib.org/view?docId=tf0f59n4t0&chunk.id=bioghist-1.8.3&brand=oac
|title = Guide to the Hammer and Coffin Society Records, 1906–1987
|publisher = Online Archive of California}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|title = Bradley Efron
|journal = Significance
|doi=10.1111/j.1740-9713.2010.00460.x
|volume=7
|issue = 4|year=2010
|pages=178–181
|author=Champkin Julian|s2cid = 247667658}}</ref>

He is currently a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at Stanford. At Stanford he has been the Chair of the Department of Statistics, Associate Dean of the School of Humanities and Sciences, Chairman of the University Advisory Board, Chair of the Faculty Senate, and co-director of the undergraduate-level Mathematical & Computational Science Program.

Efron holds the Max H. Stein endowed chair as Professor of Humanities and Sciences at Stanford.

He has made many important contributions to many areas of statistics. Efron's work has spanned both theoretical and applied topics, including empirical Bayes analysis (with [[Carl Morris (statistician)|Carl Morris]]), applications of [[differential geometry]] to [[statistical inference]], the analysis of survival data, and inference for microarray gene expression data.<ref>{{cite book|author = Bradley Efron|title = Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction|publisher = Institute of Mathematical Statistics Monographs/Cambridge University Press|year = 2010|isbn=9780521192491}}</ref> He is the author of a classic monograph, ''The Jackknife, the Bootstrap and Other Resampling Plans'' (1982) and has also co-authored (with [[Robert Tibshirani]]) the text ''An Introduction to the Bootstrap'' (1994).

He created a set of [[intransitive dice]] called [[Efron's dice]].<ref name="MathWorld">{{cite web |last1=Weisstein |first1=Eric W. |title=Efron's Dice |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/EfronsDice.html |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |access-date=12 January 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Non-transitive Dice |url=https://www.cut-the-knot.org/Probability/NonTransitiveDice.shtml |website=www.cut-the-knot.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Savage |first1=Richard P. |title=The Paradox of Nontransitive Dice |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=May 1994 |volume=101 |issue=5 |pages=429–436 |doi=10.2307/2974903 |jstor=2974903 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2974903}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rump |first1=Christopher M. |title=Strategies for Rolling the Efron Dice |journal=Mathematics Magazine |date=June 2001 |volume=74 |issue=3 |pages=212–216 |doi=10.2307/2690722 |jstor=2690722 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2690722 |access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref>

==Awards==
Efron has been given many honors, including a [[MacArthur Prize Fellowship]], membership in the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], fellowship in the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] (IMS) and the [[American Statistical Association]] (ASA), the [[Lester R. Ford Award]],<ref>{{cite journal|author=Efron, Bradley|title=Controversies in the Foundations of Statistics|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|year=1978|volume=85|issue=4|pages=231–246|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/controversies-in-the-foundations-of-statistics|doi=10.2307/2321163|jstor=2321163}}</ref> the [[Wilks Memorial Award|Wilks Medal]], the [[Parzen Prize]], and the [[C. R. Rao#In his honour|Rao Prize]], [[R. A. Fisher Lectureship|Fisher]], Rietz, and Wald lecturer.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.imstat.org/awards/lectures.htm |title=Awards - Special Lectures Info, Institute of Mathematical Statistics |access-date=2015-01-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221081412/http://www.imstat.org/awards/lectures.htm |archive-date=2015-02-21 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2005, he was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]], the highest scientific honor by the United States, for his exceptional work in the field of Statistics (especially for his inventing of the bootstrap resampling technique).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5300000000429|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121016083947/https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5300000000429|archive-date=2012-10-16|work=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details|title=Bradley Efron|publisher=National Science Foundation|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was presented with the award on May 29, 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/2005nmslaureates_pressrelease.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107133525/https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/2005nmslaureates_pressrelease.pdf|archive-date=2016-01-07|title=President Bush announces the recipients of the 2005 National Medal of Science|publisher=Office of Science and Technology Policy|via=National Science Foundation|date=May 29, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2014, he was awarded the [[Guy Medal]] in Gold.

In 2016, Efron was chosen to receive the [[BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award]] in the Basic Sciences category jointly with [[David Cox (statistician)|David Cox]], for the development of “pioneering and hugely influential” statistical methods, in Efron's case again especially the bootstrap resampling technique.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bradley Efron, 9th Frontiers of Knowledge Award in Basic Sciences |url=https://www.frontiersofknowledgeawards-fbbva.es/galardonados/bradley-efron-2/ |access-date=2026-07-27 |website=Premios Fronteras |language=en}}</ref>

He received the [[International Prize in Statistics]] at the 2019 [[World Statistics Congress]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://statprize.org/index.cfm|title=International Prize in Statistics Awarded to Stanford's Bradley Efron|date=2018-11-12}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Keystone pipeline blocked, statistics prize and horse cull|journal=Nature|date=14 November 2018 |pages=298–299|volume=563|issue=7731|doi=10.1038/d41586-018-07349-2|pmid=30429573|bibcode=2018Natur.563..298.|doi-access=free}}</ref>
